hints.junior: Coverage only answers whether the code ran. Mutation testing answers whether a bug in it would actually get caught.
hints.mid: Mutating the whole codebase overnight turns a 5-minute CI run into 3 hours, and most survived mutants come from files where it barely matters.
hints.staff: The one mutant that mattered, a missing idempotency check, was in there the whole time — buried as one line in a two-hundred-line report nobody fully read.

hints.junior: Click Run mutation testing in each mode and see how long it takes and whether the real bug is easy to find.
hints.mid: Mutating everything buries the real survivor under hundreds of low-value ones. Scoping to the high-risk modules puts it front and center in minutes.
hints.staff: Same injected bug in both runs — only the amount of surrounding noise, and therefore whether anyone notices it, changes.

hints.junior: A mutant that survives means the tests wouldn't notice if the code actually changed that way — a much stronger signal than 'this line ran.'
hints.mid: The cost is combinatorial, not linear — a handful of conditionals in one file can generate dozens of mutants, each needing its own full test run.
hints.staff: Some survived mutants are equivalent code changes that can never be killed by any test — chasing 100% past a reasonable point is its own narrower version of the same overkill.

hints.junior: Point mutation testing at the folders where a missed bug is actually expensive — payments, auth — not the whole repository.
hints.mid: Incremental runs re-mutate only changed files, or run the scoped set as a nightly job instead of blocking every PR.
hints.staff: Treat the mutation score target as scoped too — a high bar makes sense for money-handling code, and produces busywork chasing equivalent mutants everywhere else.

sections.junior: Today's case is about a payment bug that had full test coverage and still shipped, and about the tool built to catch exactly that kind of gap, and what happens when a team points it at everything at once.
sections.mid: Coverage only tells you whether a line ran during a test. Mutation testing tells you whether a test would actually notice if that line's behavior changed.
sections.staff: The one mutant that mattered was really there the whole time, sitting in a report with two hundred other entries that nobody had time to read all the way through.

sections.junior: Mutation testing makes small deliberate changes to the code and reruns the real test suite against each one, and if the tests still pass, that's a gap worth knowing about.
sections.mid: The cost isn't linear, it's combinatorial — a handful of conditions in one file can produce dozens of mutants, and each one needs its own full test run to check.
sections.staff: Not every survived mutant is a real gap either, some are equivalent to the original code in every observable way and can never be killed, so chasing a perfect score past a certain point stops being useful.

sections.junior: Run the same underlying bug through both scopes and watch how long each takes and how easy the real result is to spot.
sections.mid: Mutating everything produces hundreds of low-value survivors that bury the one that matters. Scoping to the high-risk modules puts that same survivor front and center.
sections.staff: It's the identical injected bug in both runs — the only thing that changes between them is how much noise is standing between it and someone actually reading it.

sections.junior: Mutation testing catches gaps coverage can't see, but running it on everything buries the result that actually matters under noise nobody reads.
sections.mid: Scope it to a small set of genuinely high-risk modules so a real survived mutant is a short report, not one line among hundreds.
sections.staff: Match the mutation score target to where a gap is genuinely expensive — chasing a perfect score everywhere is its own quieter version of the same mistake.
